title: What Is Man That You Watch Him So?
summary: Job finishes his reply to Eliphaz by describing his life as forced labor, sleepless nights, and a body covered in sores, all passing as quickly as a breath. Then he turns from his friends and speaks straight to God, asking why God guards him like a sea monster, terrifies him in dreams, and will not look away long enough for him to swallow. He ends by asking why God does not simply pardon him before he disappears into the dust.
story: Job has lost his wealth, his ten children, and his health (chapters 1 and 2). Three friends came to comfort him, sat in silence for seven days, and then listened as Job cursed the day he was born (chapter 3). Eliphaz answered first, gently but firmly suggesting that the innocent do not perish and that Job should accept God's discipline (chapters 4 and 5). Chapter 6 began Job's reply, aimed mostly at friends who had failed him. Chapter 7 carries that reply to its end, and something important happens along the way: Job stops talking about God and begins talking to him. From here on the book's great argument is not only between Job and his friends but between Job and God himself.
historical:
The book of Job gives no date for its events or its writing. Job lives in the land of Uz (1:1), a place outside Israel, probably somewhere to the east or southeast in the region associated with Edom or northern Arabia. He offers sacrifices himself as head of his household, measures wealth in livestock, and lives a long life, details that give the story a setting like that of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The date of composition is a separate question. Some place the book in the time of Solomon, when Israel's wisdom writing flourished; many scholars date it between the seventh and fourth centuries BC, often to the period of the Babylonian exile or after; others argue for an early origin. The Hebrew of the poetry is difficult and full of rare words, which is one reason dating is hard.

Job's complaint belongs to a wider conversation in the ancient Near East. Mesopotamian scribes produced poems about a righteous sufferer, such as the Babylonian work known by its opening words, Ludlul bel nemeqi (I Will Praise the Lord of Wisdom), in which a man describes sickness, sleeplessness, and abandonment before his god restores him. Job's lament shares that world's vocabulary of bodily misery, but it is far more daring in addressing its questions directly to the one God.
cultural:
Job's opening pictures come from ordinary economic life. The hired hand worked for a daily wage, and Israel's law required that he be paid before sunset because he depended on it (Deuteronomy 24:14-15). The slave had no wage at all and longed only for the shade at the end of a day in the sun. Job's months feel like that: work with no reward and no end. The weaver's shuttle in verse 6 was the tool that carried the thread back and forth across the loom, flying fast, and a thread cut from the loom was a common ancient picture of a life ended.

Verse 12 draws on imagery shared across the region. In texts from ancient Ugarit, a city on the Syrian coast, the storm god Baal fights Yam, the Sea, and chaos monsters of the deep. Israel's poets sometimes used this imagery to describe the LORD's rule over every rebellious power (Psalm 74:13-14). Job asks whether he is such a threat that God must set a guard over him. Sheol (verse 9) was the Hebrew name for the realm of the dead, the shadowy place below where all the dead went, pictured as a land of no return.
literary: Chapter 7 is poetry, written like nearly all of Job's speeches in parallel lines where the second half restates, sharpens, or extends the first. It moves in two parts. Verses 1-10 are general lament about the human condition, spoken about man and about Job. Verse 11 is the hinge: “Therefore I will not restrain my mouth,” and from there Job addresses God as You. The most striking move is in verses 17-18, which echo Psalm 8. That psalm marvels, what is man that God is mindful of him? Job asks the same question with bitter irony: “What is man that You should exalt him, that You should set Your heart upon him,” and then answers that God's attention means testing every moment. The chapter also runs on the image of breath (verses 7 and 16), framing Job's life as something brief and weightless.

outline.t: Life as forced labor and sleepless nights
A life like a breath that goes down to Sheol
Job turns to God: why guard me like the sea?
What is man, that you watch him so closely?

doctrines.note: The chapter gives voice to suffering without tidying it up. Scripture includes this complaint in full, which tells readers that bringing pain honestly before God is not outside the life of faith.

Human life is brief and fragile, a breath and a passing cloud. Job's twisted echo of Psalm 8 raises the question of human worth from the underside: if God cares about human beings, why does that care feel like surveillance?
Job's words in verses 11-21 are addressed to God, not merely about him. Complaint spoken to God is still a form of prayer, the same form found in many psalms of lament.

words.note: Hevel, breath or vapor, the word that runs through Ecclesiastes (often translated vanity or meaningless). Here in verse 16 it describes Job's days as insubstantial, gone as soon as they appear. The same idea is voiced in verse 7 with a different word, ruach, breath or wind.

Sheol, the realm of the dead in the Old Testament, the place all the dead go, righteous and wicked alike. It is not the later idea of hell as a place of punishment. For Job it means the end of return, work, and remembrance, which is why he wants God to act now.

Paqad, to visit, attend to, or inspect. The verb can describe God's gracious visitation or his inspection for judgment. In verse 18 Job uses it of God attending to him every morning, and the irony is sharp: the care that should be a comfort feels like an inspector's audit.
Miphga, target, a rare word from a root meaning to strike or meet. In verse 20 Job pictures himself as the mark God keeps hitting, an image he will return to in later speeches.

christ: The link here is thematic, not predictive. The question “What is man?” from Psalm 8, which Job turns inside out, is taken up in Hebrews 2:6-9, where the writer says we do not yet see everything subject to humanity, but we do see Jesus, crowned with glory because he suffered death. Jesus himself prayed from the depth of anguish, and on the cross spoke the opening line of a psalm of abandonment (Mark 15:34, quoting Psalm 22:1). The New Testament says he can sympathize with human weakness because he was tempted in every way as we are (Hebrews 4:15). Job's final question, why God does not simply pardon and take away iniquity, is one the Christian story answers in the cross, though Job himself cannot see that answer.

hard.q: Is Job sinning when he speaks to God this way?
hard.a: Job accuses God of guarding him like an enemy, hounding him, and refusing to look away. Many readers find this shocking, and the friends think it is dangerous talk. Yet the book frames Job's words carefully. The narrator says that in all his early trials Job did not sin with his lips (2:10), and at the end God tells Eliphaz that the friends have not spoken rightly about him as Job has (42:7). Interpreters read that verdict in different ways. Some think God approves Job's honesty and his refusal to pretend, while not endorsing every accusation; God does rebuke Job's words without knowledge in chapters 38 to 41, and Job repents (42:6). Others emphasize that Job, unlike his friends, kept speaking to God rather than only about him. Either way, the book does not treat lament as unbelief. Job's protest assumes that God is real, just, and the one to whom he must speak. When Job says he would prefer death to life in his body (verse 15), the book records his anguish without recommending it; a reader who shares that longing should not carry it alone, and should reach out now to a trusted friend, a pastor, a doctor, or a crisis line.

questions: Job moves from speaking about God to speaking to God. What difference does that shift make in how you handle your own complaints?
Job turns Psalm 8's wonder into a bitter question. When has God's closeness felt more like pressure than comfort to you, and what did you do with that feeling?
Job says, “my life is but a breath.” How does taking the brevity of life seriously change what you ask of God and of others?
